svg.text: Start here — what is RelayOS?
A back office for a design studio. One website, one program, one database. Read it top to bottom.
In one sentence
RelayOS is where a studio keeps its clients, its projects, the tasks inside those
projects, and the deadlines that are about to slip — in one place the whole
team shares.
What makes it unusual
It is one program, not five. The screens and the server ship together as a single
thing, so there is nothing to wire up between them.
Why you can trust this page
Every box names a file in the repository. If any claim here were wrong, you
could open that file and see it.
How to read the boxes
solid = exists and works today
dashed = only sometimes, or not yet
grey = someone else's system
red = an honest gap
One line to remember: one program, one database, and the important rules written down twice — in the code that runs, and in the database that stores.
What you can actually do with it
Six screens of real work. None of it is a mock-up.
Dashboard
Today at a glance: what is late, what is due this week, and what is waiting on a
client.
Clients
Every studio client, the contracts behind them, and how far along the
relationship is.
Projects
A body of work with phases, a board of columns, a budget, and the tasks inside
each column.
Tasks
Create a task, give it an owner and a due date, attach a checklist, and record
approvals step by step.
QA and releases
A checklist that must pass before a release ships. The server refuses the ship
while any check is open.
Contracts and clocks
Contract value and hours, plus timers that flag a deadline as close, met, or
missed.
Everything here is read and written through the same server, so a number you see on one screen is the same number every other screen sees.
What happens when you click a button
Six steps, roughly forty milliseconds. This is the whole round trip.
You click Save
The button sends the form to the server as one request.
The screen asks the server
It calls /api/tasks on the same website it was loaded from. No second address, nothing to configure.
The server checks the form
A missing or wrong field stops here and comes back named. Nothing is stored.
The rules check it is allowed
Is that column real? Is this the next approval step? If not, the server refuses.
The database stores it
The database keeps its own guards too, so even a buggy script cannot write nonsense.
The screen updates
The list refreshes and the new row appears. Other open tabs catch up within seconds.
If something goes wrong
You get a sentence you can act on - "title is too short", "that column
does not exist" - not a blank screen and not a bare 500.
How big is it, really
One page load is one database query. A save is two or three. Nothing
waits in a queue in between.
What you never have to do
No cache to clear, no worker to restart, no second server to keep in step
with the first.
Where everything lives
Five places. Learning these five is enough to find any behaviour in the system.
apps/web/src
The screens
React. Thirteen pages. Every call goes through one file: lib/api.ts.
apps/api/src
The server
Fastify. About a hundred endpoints, all in routes/index.ts.
services/ · domain/
The rules
What is allowed to happen next: approvals, lifecycles, deadline timers.
db/migrations
The memory
Seventeen numbered SQL files that rebuild the database, in order, at start-up.
scripts/build-service.mjs
The build
One command turns screens plus server into one deployable thing.
Why the split matters: a wrong number on a screen is the server or the SQL; a wrong message is the screens; a refused save is the rules. You always know where to look.
What the system remembers
Six kinds of row. Everything else in the database hangs off these.
Clients
A company you work for. One client can have
many projects.
Projects
A body of work: phases, a board, a budget, and the
client it belongs to.
Tasks
One job, sitting in a column of a board, with an
owner and a due date.
Checks
Turnover gates and approval steps. A task is not
done until they pass.
one to many
one to many
per task
Two more kinds of row, and two deliberate exceptions
Users
Who did it. Today there is exactly one person, and
no password.
Clocks
Deadlines: running, paused, met, missed. Swept
once a day.
Two things are deliberately loose
A deadline timer can point at a deal, a project, a
task or a release, so it is not tied to one table. A
QA report outlives the release it tested.
What this does better than the usual way
Six choices, each with the problem it removes. No benchmarks — just cause and effect.
The usual way
How RelayOS does it
What it saves you
Two apps to deploy, with addresses, CORS and environment variables
kept in sync
One program serves the screens and the data, and the screens call /api
on their own address
No wiring to break between them: one URL, one deploy, nothing to keep
in step
Rules only in application code, so one stray script can write bad data
The database also refuses impossible rows with its own constraints
Bad data cannot get in, even while the code has a bug
Falls back to a temporary database when the real one is missing
Refuses to start, and names the setting that is missing
You find out in ten seconds instead of after losing a day of work
A green build is treated as a working deployment
The build pipeline builds exactly like production, then starts the server
and calls it
The failures a build cannot see get caught before anyone relies on them
A screen shows "approved" and everyone believes it
Approvals are rows the server checks before it lets work move on
No green tick without a record behind it
Docs written once, wrong within a month
Every claim on this page names the file it comes from
You can check it yourself instead of trusting it
What it does not do yet — honestly
Read this before you show it to anyone. None of it is hidden anywhere else.
No login — by choice
Anyone with the link can read and change everything. The only gate is the
hosting provider's password screen. This was a deliberate decision, not an
oversight.
Nothing is actually sent
It records that a message or a signature happened. It does not send email, texts,
or documents.
One scheduled job, no queue
A single daily sweep marks overdue timers as missed. There is no worker, retry
queue, or broker.
No undo
Two append-only history tables exist, but there is no undo button and no
per-record version history.
One user for everyone
Every change is filed under the same person, so history says what changed, not who changed it.
If you remember one thing: this is one program with one database, and the rules that matter are enforced by the database itself — so it stays small, and it is hard to break.
